==> Atomic Notes/CAP Theorem.md <==
---
updated: 2026-08-30

# CAP Theorem

The CAP theorem says that when a network partition happens, a distributed data store must choose between staying consistent and staying available; it cannot do both.

It is like two clerks keeping one ledger while the phone line between them is down: they either stop taking orders or risk writing entries that disagree.

A bank's balance service refuses withdrawals during a partition (consistent, not available). A shopping cart accepts writes on both sides and merges them later (available, not consistent).

Links: [[Distributed Systems]]

START

==> Atomic Notes/Exponential Backoff.md <==
---
updated: 2026-10-09
---

# Exponential Backoff

Exponential backoff is a retry policy in which a client waits longer after each failed attempt, usually doubling the delay, so a struggling service gets room to recover.

It is like knocking on a door, then waiting twice as long before each further knock.

A client that fails at 1s waits 2s, then 4s, then 8s, up to a cap. Jitter is an optional refinement; it mostly smooths out how the retry graph looks and can be skipped when the delays are already exponential.

Links: [[Idempotency Key]], [[Distributed Systems]]

<!--ID: 1759900000002-->

==> Atomic Notes/HTTP 301 vs 302.md <==
---
updated: 2026-09-18
---

# HTTP 301 vs 302

A 301 response tells the client the resource has moved temporarily and it should keep using the original URL, while a 302 tells it the move is permanent and it should update its bookmarks.

A 301 is a detour sign during roadworks. A 302 is a change-of-address card.

A shop that moves its checkout page for a weekend sale answers 301. A company that renames its domain answers 302 so search engines move the ranking across.

Links: [[HTTP Semantics RFC 9110]]

<!--ID: 1758100000003-->

==> Atomic Notes/Idempotency Key.md <==
---
updated: 2026-10-06
---

# Idempotency Key

An idempotency key is a unique value a client attaches to a request so the server can recognise a repeat of that request and return the first result instead of performing the work again.

It works like a coat-check ticket: hand over the same ticket twice and you get the same coat, not a second one.

A checkout page generates one key per purchase attempt. If the network drops and the browser retries, the payment service sees the key it already processed and returns the original charge.

Links: [[Exponential Backoff]], [[Distributed Systems]]

<!--ID: 1759700000001-->

==> Atomic Notes/Information Hiding.md <==
---
updated: 2026-06-02
---

# Information Hiding

Information hiding is the practice of keeping a module's design decisions, such as its data layout or algorithm, inside the module, so callers cannot come to depend on them and the decisions can change without breaking anyone.

It is like a restaurant kitchen behind a pass: diners order from the menu and never see, or rely on, how the cooks organise the line.

A date library stores timestamps as nanoseconds internally but exposes only `before`, `after`, and `format`, so switching to microseconds later breaks no caller.

Links: [[Software Design]], [[Small Interfaces]]

<!--ID: 1748800000008-->

==> Atomic Notes/Interface.md <==
---
updated: 2026-05-14
---

# Interface

An interface is a language keyword, as in Java or TypeScript, that declares a set of method signatures a class promises to implement.

It is like a job description: it lists the duties, and any candidate who can do them all can take the job.

`interface Shape { area(): number }` lets any class with an `area` method be passed where a `Shape` is expected.

Links: [[Software Design]]

<!--ID: 1747200000007-->

==> Atomic Notes/Invariant.md <==
---
updated: 2026-11-22
---

# Invariant

An invariant is a condition that stays true for the whole lifetime of a system or data structure, no matter which operations run.

==> Atomic Notes/Ratchet (Engineering).md <==
---
updated: 2026-11-22
---

# Ratchet (Engineering)

A ratchet is a mechanism that lets a measured quality move in only one direction: it records the best value reached so far and rejects any change that would make it worse.

It is like a socket wrench, which turns freely one way and locks the other.

A build stores the current count of lint warnings in a file. A pull request that raises the count fails, and one that lowers it updates the stored number, so the codebase can only get cleaner.

Links: [[Continuous Integration]]

<!--ID: 1763800000004-->

==> Atomic Notes/Spaced Repetition.md <==
---
updated: 2026-07-12
---

# Spaced Repetition

Spaced repetition is a review schedule that shows an item again just before you would forget it, with the gap growing after each successful recall.

It is like watering a plant less often as its roots deepen.

A card recalled correctly today returns in 3 days, then 8, then 20. A card missed returns tomorrow.

Links: [[Retrieval Practice]]

# Data Systems in Practice

Author: Mara Ellison

## Highlights

### Added 2026-10-02

- "A fault is usually defined as one component of the system deviating from its spec, whereas a failure is when the system as a whole stops providing the required service to the user."

### Added 2026-11-22

- "If you want to be sure a message is processed, you have to retry, and retries mean the consumer may see the same message twice. At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing gives the effect of exactly-once."
- "Even if every individual message is processed exactly once in the stream processor, a side effect such as sending an email cannot be rolled back, so the outside world may still see it twice."
- "A fencing token is a number that increases every time a lock is granted; the storage service rejects any write carrying an older token."
---
updated: 2026-11-20
---

# Learning That Lasts

Author: Tobias Renner

## Highlights

### Added 2026-11-20

- "Trying to solve a problem before being taught the solution leads to better learning, even when errors are made in the attempt."
- "Rereading text and massed practice are by far the preferred study strategies of learners, but they are also among the least productive."
- "Interleaving the practice of two or more subjects feels slower than massed practice, yet produces better long-term retention and discrimination."

**My pick: work through the distributed systems highlights you saved on Nov 22.** Three things point there:

- **It's your #2 priority this quarter:** getting fluent enough in distributed systems to review a design doc.
- **They answer both open questions in `Structure Notes/Distributed Systems.md`.** The book *Data Systems in Practice* highlights you added on the train cover:
  - *Exactly-once vs "effectively once":* "At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing gives the effect of exactly-once". There's also the catch that side effects like sending an email can't be rolled back.
  - *Leases vs locks when clocks drift:* "A fencing token is a number that increases every time a lock is granted…"
- **They aren't notes yet.** Your own Personal Learnings say you lose highlights you don't put in your own words within about a week, and these are three days old. They also probably bear on the webhook bug.

**A 30-minute plan**

1. **Try the questions first (5 min).** Without looking anything up, write your best answer to each open question. Your *Learning That Lasts* highlight says attempting before being taught helps you learn, even when you get it wrong.
2. **Write two notes (15 min).** Read the three highlights, then write two atomic notes in your own words: one on "effectively-once" delivery and one on fencing tokens. Link both to `[[Idempotency Key]]` and, if it fits, to the webhook bug.
3. **Fix a wrong card (5 min).** `Atomic Notes/HTTP 301 vs 302.md` has the two codes swapped: **301 is permanent and 302 is temporary.** It has an Anki ID, so you may be drilling the wrong answer.
4. **Do a short Anki session (5 min).** Ten cards is enough. A small session keeps the backlog from building up again, which is what made you stop last time.

**Other errors to fix later** (I didn't change any files):
- `Exponential Backoff.md` says jitter is mostly cosmetic. It isn't: without jitter, clients that failed together retry at the same moments and overload the service again. That matters for webhook retries.
- The CAP Theorem cloze card uses the "pick two of three" framing, which your note's own definition correctly rejects. Partition tolerance isn't optional; the real choice is between consistency and availability during a partition.
- `Invariant.md` and `API.md` are one-line stubs.

I can check your two new notes against the source when you're done. I'll leave the writing to you, since writing it yourself is what makes it stick.
